lesson.title: Parallel Lines and the System With No Answer
lesson.summary: An inconsistent system is one with no solution at all, which happens algebraically when eliminating a variable leads to a false numerical statement, and geometrically when the lines are parallel and never meet.
lesson.body:
Not every system has a solution. When no ordered pair can make every equation in the system true at the same time, the system is called inconsistent. This is the opposite of the consistent systems from the previous section, where at least one shared point always existed; here, no such point exists anywhere on the coordinate plane, no matter how far you extend the lines in either direction or how carefully you search. It is important to remember that inconsistent does not mean the equations were written wrong; it simply describes a real relationship between two lines that happen never to cross.

The geometric cause is almost always the same: the two lines are parallel. Parallel lines share the same slope but have different y-intercepts, so they run alongside each other forever without ever touching. Since a solution of a system requires a point that lies on both lines simultaneously, and parallel lines share no points, a system made of two distinct parallel lines is guaranteed to be inconsistent, and this holds true regardless of how the equations happen to be written or scaled. If the two equations described the same line instead of merely parallel ones, the system would be dependent rather than inconsistent, which is why matching slopes alone is not enough; the intercepts must also be checked.

Consider the system 2x + 3y = 6 and 4x + 6y = 18. Rewriting each in slope-intercept form reveals the slopes: from 2x + 3y = 6, subtracting 2x and dividing by 3 gives y = (-2/3)x + 2. From 4x + 6y = 18, subtracting 4x and dividing by 6 gives y = (-2/3)x + 3. Both lines have the same slope, -2/3, but different y-intercepts, 2 and 3, so the lines are parallel and distinct, meaning they never intersect no matter how far they are extended.

This can also be confirmed algebraically without graphing. Multiply the first equation by 2 to get 4x + 6y = 12, which has the same left side as the second equation, 4x + 6y = 18. Subtracting one from the other gives (4x + 6y) - (4x + 6y) = 12 - 18, which simplifies to 0 = -6. That is a false statement no matter what x and y are, and reaching a false numerical statement while trying to eliminate a variable is the algebraic signature of an inconsistent system: it means no ordered pair can ever satisfy both equations at once. This algebraic shortcut is often faster and more reliable than graphing, especially when the lines are close together and hard to tell apart by eye.

Because inconsistent systems have zero solutions, the labels independent and dependent, which describe how many solutions a consistent system has, simply do not apply to them. Independent and dependent both assume a system already has at least one solution to classify; an inconsistent system never clears that first hurdle, so it stands as its own category, separate from the ones explored next, and every linear system of two equations in two variables falls into exactly one of these three categories: inconsistent, independent, or dependent.
